The Western pond turtle Actinemys marmorata is a comparatively small-bodied freshwater emydid, with females attaining a maximum carapace length of 14.8 cm [Li = 14.8 cm] in adulthood, while males grow to a slightly larger ultimate carapace length of 16 cm [Li = 16 cm]. This reversed sexual size dimorphism, where males are the larger sex, is unusual among North American pond turtles and is thought to relate to male-male combat during the breeding season. Hatchlings emerge from their nests weighing approximately 5 grams [Wwb = approximately 5 grams], a modest neonatal mass that is typical of small-bodied chelonians with a semi-aquatic lifestyle. The relatively diminutive size at emergence, coupled with high rates of nest predation by raccoons and skunks, means that first-year mortality is substantial and represents a major demographic bottleneck. Delayed maturity is a common life-history strategy in this species, and data from long-term field studies in California indicate that puberty is attained at a carapace length of 13.4 cm [Lp = 13.4 cm], a threshold that usually corresponds to an age of between 10 and 12 years depending on local growing season length and resource availability.

At a constant incubation temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], which approximates the cooler conditions encountered in shaded or deep nests at the northern edge of the species range, gravid females produce a maximum of approximately 1.5 clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately 1.5 clutches per year], with each clutch containing up to 6.3 eggs [N_R_i = each clutch containing up to 6.3 eggs]. The resulting annual reproductive output, while modest in absolute terms, represents a considerable energetic investment for a turtle of this body size. These reproductive parameters were documented during a multi-year captive breeding study at the San Francisco Zoo, where females were maintained under controlled thermal and photoperiod regimes that mimicked natural conditions. The eggs themselves are parchment-shelled and undergo a relatively long incubation period that can exceed 100 days at lower temperatures, with the precise duration depending on the thermal profile of the nest chamber. This extended embryogenesis period likely allows for greater yolk absorption and may contribute to the production of more robust hatchlings that have a better chance of surviving their first winter dormancy period.

Adult females reach a maximum ultimate wet weight of 563 grams [Wwi = 563 grams], which is substantially lower than the corresponding value for adult males, who typically achieve an ultimate wet weight of 626 grams [Wwi = 626 grams] under favorable foraging conditions. This divergence in asymptotic mass reflects not only the differences in carapace length but also a tendency for males to develop deeper, more heavily muscled bodies that aid in intraspecific combat and territory defense. Growth curves fitted to mark-recapture data from a protected population in Sonoma County, California, revealed that individuals continue to increase in mass slowly even after reaching sexual maturity, with somatic growth rate declining asymptotically toward zero only once the animal approaches its maximum dimensions. The difference in size between the sexes is not apparent at birth, as all neonates emerge at a similar wet weight at birth of 5 grams [Wwb = 5 grams], but becomes increasingly conspicuous after the first several years of growth. It is noteworthy that the overall body size of this species is considerably smaller than that of the closely related pond slider Trachemys scripta, a difference that is thought to reflect the cooler, less productive aquatic habitats typically occupied by Actinemys marmorata.

Maximum lifespan data for the Western pond turtle, recorded from captive individuals maintained at a constant temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], indicate that the species is capable of surviving for up to 80 years [am = up to 80 years], making it one of the longer-lived freshwater turtles in North America. This delayed senescence pattern is consistent with the species low annual reproductive output and its reliance on high adult survival to maintain population stability, a classic slow life-history strategy typical of long-lived reptiles. In the wild, the oldest reliably documented individual was a male from a population in the Willamette Valley of Oregon that was estimated from growth annuli to be at least 67 years old at the time of capture. The extended lifespan, combined with a late age at first breeding, means that adult turtles must survive for many decades to replace themselves in the population, and even small increases in adult mortality from roadkill, drought, or predation can have profound negative effects on population viability. Conservation efforts therefore focus heavily on protecting adult habitat and reducing threats to the oldest, most reproductively valuable individuals in the population.

When interpreting these life-history measurements, it is important to note that asymptotic body size parameters, such as the female ultimate carapace length of 14.8 cm [Li = 14.8 cm] and the male ultimate carapace length of 16 cm [Li = 16 cm], represent population-level averages that may mask considerable local variation depending on habitat quality and hydrologic regime. In productive, permanent pond systems with abundant aquatic invertebrates and amphibian larvae, adult turtles frequently exceed these dimensions by several millimeters, whereas individuals occupying ephemeral or degraded streams often fall short. Similarly, the ultimate wet weight values of 563 grams [Wwi = 563 grams] for females and 626 grams [Wwi = 626 grams] for males are best understood as benchmarks against which the condition of individual turtles can be assessed during health monitoring programs. The consistency of the age at puberty as a function of body length (13.4 cm [Lp = 13.4 cm]) across disparate geographic populations suggests that this species possesses a fixed developmental threshold, whereby an individual must reach a critical body size before initiating the hormonal cascades that lead to gonadal maturation and first reproduction.
